editorNote: Atari answers a battered game market with backward compatibility, while PC databases, low-cost business micros and dial-up security crowd a consequential week.
morningLine: Monday, May 21, 1984: Atari bets that a new console can carry yesterday’s cartridges into tomorrow’s arcade.

lead.headline: Atari Bets on Compatibility with $140 7800 ProSystem
lead.dek: A sharper arcade-style machine promises to preserve the vast Atari 2600 cartridge shelf.
lead.confidence: Exact-date announcement; later release history supplied for context
body: Atari unveiled the 7800 ProSystem on May 21, pitching a $140 console as the company’s answer to a home videogame business shaken by falling sales and crowded store shelves. The new machine promised more elaborate arcade-style action while meeting owners on familiar ground: it could also play Atari 2600 cartridges.

That compatibility was the heart of the wager. Millions of older cartridges already sat beneath American television sets, and Atari was asking families to upgrade without abandoning them. The system, designed by General Computer Corporation, paired that library with graphics hardware promoted as capable of moving roughly 100 objects on screen.

Atari’s announcement placed games back at the center of its consumer strategy just as retailers and publishers were questioning the console market. An advertised launch price of $140 put the ProSystem above bargain machines but below the cost of a complete home-computer setup.

The unveiling would prove to be only the beginning of a delayed story. Atari’s ownership transition stalled the intended 1984 rollout, and the 7800 did not reach broad U.S. commercial release until 1986. This week, however, its promise was immediate: better arcade pictures without making the old cartridge box obsolete.

stories.headline: Ashton-Tate Unwraps dBASE III for IBM PCs
body: Ashton-Tate introduced dBASE III as a major expansion of the database package that had become a business standard on microcomputers. The PC-DOS release claimed capacity beyond two billion records, hardware permitting, with 128 fields per record and access to ten databases at once.

New date and memo fields brought date arithmetic and text entries up to 4,000 bytes. Menus, online help, full-screen editing, report generation, color setup and programmable keys aimed to make that increased reach manageable from an office desktop.

stories.headline: NEC Breaks the $2,000 Barrier for a Complete 16-bit Business Micro
body: NEC Information Systems brought a complete 16-bit business microcomputer below $2,000, a threshold Computerworld said no other major micro vendor had crossed. The machine was headed for the Comdex/Spring exhibition opening May 22 in Atlanta.

The low price sharpened competition for buyers who wanted a business-ready system rather than a bare starter configuration. NEC’s concurrent endorsement of Unix also showed how strongly standardized operating environments were pulling at the fragmented microcomputer market.

stories.headline: Telemail Intrusions Put Online Security on the Front Page
stories.confidence: Same-week report with exact-date security response
body: Four people were arraigned over allegations of illegally entering GTE Telenet’s Telemail service and accessing private and U.S. government mailboxes. The case moved electronic-mail security from specialist concern to an operational problem for commercial networks.

GTE Telenet had introduced a lockout device on May 15 to bar unauthorized users. The response arrived amid growing calls for computer-crime legislation and encryption, evidence that the expanding online world was already producing a contest between access and control.
